questions.q: Why is a differential restore always at least two RESTORE statements?
options: The full backup must be restored first (WITH NORECOVERY), then the differential is restored on top of it (WITH RECOVERY)
SQL Server requires exactly two RESTORE statements for every restore, regardless of backup type
Differential backups must be split into two files before restoring
The first statement restores the log, and the second restores the data
questions.explain: A differential can't stand alone — it only contains changed pages, so the full backup underneath it must be restored first.

questions.q: What does a differential backup actually contain, per this lesson?
options: Every data page changed since the last full backup
Every data page changed since the last differential backup
Only the transaction log entries since the last backup
An exact duplicate of the full backup
questions.explain: Differentials are always relative to the last full backup, not to each other — which is why the restore chain is always exactly two backups deep.

questions.q: Why doesn't a differential restore chain ever need to stack multiple differential backups?
options: Because the most recent differential already contains everything changed since the full backup, making earlier differentials redundant
Because SQL Server only allows one differential backup to ever be taken per database
Because differentials expire after 24 hours
Because differentials must be merged manually before restoring
questions.explain: Since each differential captures all changes since the full, the latest one alone brings you fully current — no need to restore earlier differentials in between.

questions.q: What happens if you try to restore a differential backup on top of a full backup it wasn't based on?
options: SQL Server rejects the restore, using the differential_base_lsn marker to detect the mismatch
SQL Server silently merges the mismatched backups
SQL Server restores it but marks the database as corrupted with no warning
SQL Server automatically finds and restores the correct full backup instead
questions.explain: Every differential is tied to a specific full backup via an internal LSN marker; restoring it against the wrong full is rejected rather than silently applied.

questions.q: In a full-then-differential restore chain, which RESTORE statement uses `WITH RECOVERY`?
options: Only the final statement in the chain (the differential restore)
Every statement in the chain
Only the first statement (the full restore)
Neither statement — RECOVERY is applied separately afterward
questions.explain: The rule from Lesson 7 applies here too: every step except the last uses NORECOVERY, and only the final step recovers the database.
